explanations.explanation: Simon of Cyrene was just passing by on his way in from the country. Then the soldiers "forced him to carry the cross of Jesus." (Mark 15:21) Nobody asked him and he didn't volunteer. Talk about an ordinary walk turning into something he never saw coming.

explanations.answer: Lead the soldiers to the hill
explanations.explanation: I get why you'd think that, since Simon is a man coming in from the country. But the text never has him leading anybody. The soldiers did the forcing, and what they forced him to do was "carry the cross of Jesus." (Mark 15:21) The soldiers had the route covered.

No crowd control for Simon, friend. Mark doesn't give him a job like that. The soldiers forced him to carry the cross of Jesus (Mark 15:21). Simon was a man on his way in from the country, and he ended up with a load he never planned on.

I see why that sounds possible, since they did offer it. But Mark says it plainly: they offered Him wine mixed with myrrh, "but He did not take it." (Mark 15:23) The cup was held out and Jesus did not take it. So this one is False.
Yes, False. The soldiers offered Him wine mixed with myrrh, "but He did not take it." (Mark 15:23) Mark gives no reason, so I won't make one up. All we know is what He did and didn't do at Golgotha.

Right. The soldiers divided His garments "by casting lots to decide what each of them would take." (Mark 15:24) Each man's share came down to the lots. I think that's a hard thing to read, because those were His clothes.

Mark says nothing about guard duty here. The lots had a different job: they decided what each of the soldiers would take of His garments (Mark 15:24). It's a sad little scene when you picture it. I think it's one of those verses worth reading twice.

Pilate, the one who handed Jesus over to be crucified (Mark 15:15), isn't mentioned in this scene at all. The lots weren't about reports or paperwork. They were about the garments, to decide "what each of them would take." (Mark 15:24) Nothing in the text turns this into a reporting job.
That's the one. "The charge inscribed against Him read: THE KING OF THE JEWS." (Mark 15:26) Mark puts it right there in capital letters. It's the very charge, in the very words, written over Him.

That's a title you'll find elsewhere in the Gospels, but Mark 15:26 doesn't use it for the charge. The charge read: THE KING OF THE JEWS. Same kind of big title, different words. Mark keeps it exact, so we do too.
Galilee does come up later in this passage, so I see how it landed in your head. But it isn't on the charge. The charge read: THE KING OF THE JEWS (Mark 15:26).

explanations.answer: Come down from the cross and save Yourself
explanations.explanation: That's it. Those who passed by said, "come down from the cross and save Yourself!" (Mark 15:30) They were heaping abuse on Him as they said it. Mark doesn't tell us more than what they shouted, so I'll leave it right there.

explanations.answer: Call down fire from heaven on them
explanations.explanation: Nobody in this scene mentions fire, friend. What they dared Him to do was "come down from the cross and save Yourself!" (Mark 15:30) That one is all about the cross.

explanations.answer: Tear down the temple right now
explanations.explanation: The temple does come up, and that's why this one is tricky. They mentioned it just before, saying He was going to destroy it and rebuild it in three days (Mark 15:29). But the dare itself was different: "come down from the cross and save Yourself!" (Mark 15:30).

Yes, True. The chief priests and scribes said, "Let the Christ, the King of Israel, come down now from the cross, so that we may see and believe!" (Mark 15:32) Mark has them saying it among themselves. That's a lot of words about believing from people who weren't believing.

This one is True, and Mark spells it out. The chief priests and scribes said, "Let the Christ, the King of Israel, come down now from the cross, so that we may see and believe!" (Mark 15:32) They weren't saying it to Jesus directly. They were mocking Him among themselves.

That's True. Mark says, "even those who were crucified with Him berated Him." (Mark 15:32) That includes the two robbers on His right and left. At this point it seems like the whole hill was against Him.
It's actually True, friend. The verse says, "even those who were crucified with Him berated Him." (Mark 15:32) The two robbers were crucified with Him (Mark 15:27). So even they berated Him.
Yes, darkness. "From the sixth hour until the ninth hour darkness came over all the land." (Mark 15:33) Three hours of it, all over the land. Mark just states it and doesn't say more.
No hail in Mark's account, friend. What came was darkness. "From the sixth hour until the ninth hour darkness came over all the land." (Mark 15:33)

Rain would have been something you could at least carry an umbrella for. But Mark says it was darkness, not rain. "From the sixth hour until the ninth hour darkness came over all the land." (Mark 15:33)
Right. Some of those standing nearby said, "Behold, He is calling Elijah." (Mark 15:35) Elijah was a prophet of Israel. Jesus cried out "Eloi, Eloi…" and that's what they heard.

Moses, Israel's leader, is a name people know well, but Mark doesn't have the bystanders say it. They said, "Behold, He is calling Elijah." (Mark 15:35) Elijah, a prophet of Israel, is the one they named.
Abraham, Israel's forefather, never comes up in this scene. The bystanders heard "Eloi, Eloi…" and said, "Behold, He is calling Elijah." (Mark 15:35) Elijah was a prophet of Israel.
Yes, sour wine. Someone "filled a sponge with sour wine," put it on a reed and held it up for Jesus to drink (Mark 15:36). Mark names it exactly, so we keep it exact.
Water makes sense for a sponge, I'll give you that. But Mark says the sponge was filled with sour wine (Mark 15:36). That's what was held up on the reed.
A sponge full of olive oil would be quite the mess, friend, and it isn't in Mark. The sponge was filled with sour wine and held up on a reed for Jesus to drink (Mark 15:36).

That's right. "The veil of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom." (Mark 15:38) Mark puts it right after Jesus breathed His last. The veil was the temple's curtain, and it tore from the top to the bottom.
A robe being torn is something that shows up in other stories, but not here. At the temple, what was torn in two was the veil, "from top to bottom." (Mark 15:38)
No scrolls get torn in Mark's account. The text says "the veil of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom." (Mark 15:38) That's the one thing Mark names.
I see why you'd think that, since so many others mocked Him. But this centurion didn't. He said, "Truly this man was the Son of God!" (Mark 15:39) So this one is False.

Yes, False. The centurion saw how Jesus breathed His last, and then said, "Truly this man was the Son of God!" (Mark 15:39) That wasn't mocking. After all those voices heaping abuse, his was a different one.
Yes. Among the women watching from a distance was Mary Magdalene (Mark 15:40). Mark also names Mary the mother of James the younger and of Joses, and Salome.

Martha is a name you may know, the one who hosted Jesus in her home (Luke 10:38). But Mark doesn't list her among these women. The names he gives are Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James the younger and of Joses, and Salome (Mark 15:40).

Lydia, a dealer in purple cloth who listened to Paul (Acts 16:14), is from a different part of the Bible. She isn't one of the women Mark names at the cross. Mark names Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James the younger and of Joses, and Salome (Mark 15:40).
Yes, Galilee. These women "had followed Jesus and ministered to Him while He was in Galilee." (Mark 15:41) They had been with Him a good while before that hill.
Samaria is a real region, but Mark doesn't say that's where they followed Him. The text says they followed and ministered to Him "while He was in Galilee." (Mark 15:41)

Bethlehem is where Jesus was born (Matthew 2:1), so it's an understandable guess. But Mark says these women followed Jesus and ministered to Him "while He was in Galilee." (Mark 15:41) It's Galilee, not Bethlehem.
